findings.why: The simplification removed the second question but left a scenario that still constrains the answer set. The stem fixes one threat (ransomware, patient records reachable) and then asks a threat-independent question ('primarily protects AVAILABILITY'). DDoS mitigation is unambiguously an availability control by the stated criterion but does nothing for the named scenario, so the item has two defensible readings: IN if you answer the criterion, OUT if you answer the scenario. The other seven items happen to be consistent under both readings, so this single item silently decides pass/fail, and the candidate who reads the scenario most carefully is the one penalised. The phrase 'with patient records still reachable' also telegraphs the availability criterion, so the scenario adds no assessment value it could not lose.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop the scenario entirely ('Select every control that primarily protects availability'), or keep the scenario and make it govern: 'Select every control that would help keep patient records reachable during a ransomware incident' — then remove DDoS mitigation from the option list or accept it as OUT.

findings.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
findings.why: The new 'pick the most specific category, not the broadest' instruction is the wrong tie-breaker for the ISC2 canons. The canons are not nested general-to-specific; ISC2's own guidance resolves conflicts by order of precedence — Canon I outranks II, II outranks III, III outranks IV. Canon III is also the only canon that names a party ('principals'), so under a specificity rule every client-facing item routes to III. Here the actor's principal is the client and the act is refusing the principal's instruction: a candidate obeying the instruction picks Canon III, while the key is almost certainly Canon II (honesty/integrity of the report). The same inversion hits the two Canon I items — 'You report a vulnerability you found in a city's emergency dispatch system' and 'A vendor ignores your reports of a medical-device firmware flaw...' — where a specificity-minded candidate reads Canon I as the broad catch-all and drops to II or IV. The revision replaced an ambiguity with a rule that actively contradicts the authoritative resolution rule for this taxonomy.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the specificity instruction on this gate with the ISC2 precedence rule: 'If an act falls under more than one canon, choose the earliest-numbered canon that applies.' Keep the specificity wording only on taxonomies that really are general-to-specific (e.g. governance).

findings.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
findings.why: Refusing to sell by FUD is squarely Canon II (honesty) but is also the textbook Canon IV case — sensationalism and scare-selling are the practices ISC2 cites as damaging the profession's reputation, and the setting here is a sales pitch by a practitioner rather than a duty to an existing principal. Both homes are defensible from the item text alone, and the 'most specific' instruction does not separate them: neither II nor IV is narrower than the other. A candidate who reads 'sales pitch' as a profession-reputation cue answers IV and is marked wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Anchor the item to the injured party: for Canon II, '...you refuse to overstate the risk to a prospect because the claim would be untrue'; for Canon IV, move it and word it as 'you challenge a peer whose scare-marketing is bringing the profession into disrepute'.

findings.item: A signing key that never leaves the TPM chip soldered to your laptop
findings.why: The scenario rewrite added two details that pull against the intended 'something you have'. A signing key is a secret, and the item never says the key is used to authenticate to something other than the laptop it is soldered into — a possession factor bound to the very endpoint being used is normally treated as device binding, not a second factor. 'Soldered' was presumably added to signal inseparable possession but it does the opposite: it removes the separable-token property that makes 'have' obvious. The three sibling items are all textbook, so this is the only item in the bank that discriminates, and it discriminates on a distinction the bank never taught.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the token separable and the target external: 'A hardware security key you plug into the laptop to sign in to the VPN portal.' If the TPM framing is wanted, state the target explicitly ('...used to prove this laptop's identity to the corporate network').

findings.why: No gate bank in this file carries a prompt or instruction field — only 'buckets' and 'items'. The revised 'pick the most specific category rather than the broadest' rule therefore is not in the shipped item data, and candidates see bucket labels alone. That matters most here: this is a five-bucket taxonomy that genuinely is general-to-specific, and without the rule 'All production servers must run the approved hardened OS image' and 'Data at rest must be encrypted with AES-256' are both defensibly Policy (org-wide mandatory statements) or Standard (specific mandatory implementation), with no text in the item resolving which. Two of eight items turn on an instruction that is not delivered.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit 'prompt' field to the gate sites carrying the rule, e.g. 'Each statement belongs to exactly one document type. If more than one fits, choose the most specific — Standard/Procedure/Guideline before Policy.' Verify it renders before shipping.

findings.why: Availability is the standard ISC2 key and most prepared candidates will give it, but encryption-in-place is also an integrity-of-data event and modern ransomware is usually double-extortion, so a minority argue Confidentiality or Integrity. The item says only 'encrypts', with no exfiltration or alteration, which is enough to keep Availability the best answer.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the effect: 'Ransomware encrypts the file server and staff cannot open any documents.'

findings.item: Step 1: open the admin console. Step 2: select Enrol device. Step 3: scan the QR code
findings.why: The numbered-step format answers 'Procedure' by shape rather than by understanding, and 'Where practical, prefer...' does the same for Guideline while 'HIPAA' does it for Law or regulation. Three of eight items are solvable from surface form alone, so the bank over-reports mastery.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep one form-cued item as a warm-up and rewrite the others in prose that does not signal its type, e.g. 'The security team's step-by-step instructions for enrolling a new device in MDM'.

findings.why: This item is a near-verbatim repeat of the gate item 'Background checks run before a new hire starts' in the same module, as is the technical/physical framing of the distractors. A candidate who cleared the gate can answer the deep-site item from memory rather than from the branch-office context, so the site adds little discrimination over the gate.
findings.suggested_fix: Swap in an administrative control not used at the gate — e.g. 'A documented visitor sign-in and escort policy' or 'A signed data-handling agreement with the new branch's cleaning contractor'.

findings.item: An iris pattern the door camera measures against a stored template
findings.why: The rewrite produced three concept pairs (two biometrics, two knowledge secrets, two possession tokens) with identical reasoning inside each pair, so six items test three decisions. The added scenario clauses lengthen the read without adding a discrimination; the iris item is fully redundant with the fingerprint item.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace one biometric with a factor that stresses the boundary, e.g. 'A typing-rhythm profile the login page compares against your enrolled cadence' (behavioural biometric, still 'are') or a location/context factor to be explicitly excluded.

findings.item: Add a clause making the hosting provider financially responsible for data loss
findings.why: Transfer is correct and the wording ('financially responsible') is deliberately narrow, but four buckets across six items leaves Avoid and Accept with one exemplar each while Transfer gets two near-identical ones (insurance and the contract clause). Coverage is uneven rather than wrong, and a candidate cannot demonstrate the Accept/Mitigate boundary on a single item.
findings.suggested_fix: Balance to two per bucket: add an Avoid item ('Decline to take payment card data at all, and redirect customers to the processor') and a second Accept item, or drop one Transfer item.
